title: UK's scariest seance - 'alien beings, ghostly faces' and doctor banned for life
excerpt: It's been 30 years since Dr Melvyn Willin stepped into the infamous 'Scole hole' in Norfolk to commune with the dead as part of The Scole Experiment. Thirty years on, he reflects on the unnerving experience
content:
It's been 30 years since Dr Melvyn Willin stepped into the infamous 'Scole hole' in Norfolk to commune with the dead as part of The Scole Experiment. Thirty years on, he reflects on the unnerving experience

10:34, 05 Sep 2026

In the summer of 1996, psychic researcher and author Dr Melvyn Willin descended the stairs into a now-infamous basement located in the usually peaceful village of Scole, Norfolk, to talk to the dead.

‌

It was an unnerving experience that would stay with him for a lifetime, and ended with him being banned from ever returning.

‌

Over the course of five intriguing years, from 1993 to 1998, two couples, psychic researchers Sandra and Robin Foy and mediums Diana and Allen Bennett, held a series of séances with one objective in mind: to create a communication thread beyond the grave to the spirit world.

‌

A number of those who attended the notorious Scole Experiment séances reported uncanny happenings, from shocking apparitions and mysterious flashes of light to objects being moved by invisible hands.

Heavy tables were said to float, and visible spectral hands reach out and touch participants. Tape recordings, known as The Scole Tapes, captured many languages, including some believed not to be of this earth. Notably, the Foys and the Bennetts welcomed outside scrutiny, inviting sceptics and believers alike to judge for themselves whether or not the veil had truly been lifted.

‌

From 1995 to 1997, an investigation into the séances, or experimental sessions as the Scole group preferred to refer to them, was conducted by Arthur Ellison, David Fontana and Montague Keen, members of the Society for Psychical Research (SPR), a scientific organisation first established in 1882, to examine claims of paranormal phenomena.

All three members of the SPR, which takes a comparatively more scientific view when investigating claims, concluded that, after attending 20 seances over a two-year period, they'd borne witness to 'something paranormal' and hadn't detected any indication of deception.

‌

Before his visit to the Foys' 17th-century Street Farmhouse, Dr Willin, now 75, from Norfolk had been "fascinated" by the stories that were emerging from the husband-and-wife duo's pitch-black cellar.

For weeks on end, Dr Willin, who has authored books such as Ghosts Caught on Film and Music and the Paranormal, had eagerly leafed through his copies of The Spiritual Scientist, amazed by what he was hearing.

‌

He remembered: "They had everything but the kitchen sink going on there. There were apports, which are things that appear out of nowhere. There was contact with all sorts of entities through at least two of the mediums that were present there, talking about various subjects in different voices and from different slants.

"So you had the sort of lightweight ones, you had the heavyweight ones. There was a light phenomenon. There was everything, that's why it sounded so amazing."

Perhaps the most convincing aspect was the images, symbols, and elaborate writings which seemingly materialised out of nowhere on sealed rolls of photographic film, without any apparent light exposure or human interference. This included the supposed likeness of the author of Sherlock Holmes, Arthur Conan Doyle, who had passed away in 1930, as well as eerie scenes from the Victorian era, or London's St. Paul's Cathedral during the Blitz.

‌

Sometimes the images would include messages, seemingly from the dead, including 'Giuseppe Rolls sends his regards' - an apparent reference to a pioneering film professional who had worked for Polaroid before his death in 1926. Taking things a step further, the group captured images on video - known as 'Project Alice' - and produced, amongst various other startling clips, footage which showed alien-like beings.

These photographic phenomena seemingly occurred even when independent researchers were asked to select the rolls of film for themselves. An earthly hand wasn't even needed to work the camera, which would apparently click and roll away when placed on the table.

‌

Then there were the gifts, seemingly materialising out of thin air, and landing with an audible thud on the cellar table. These supposedly otherworldly offerings included old metal coins, thimbles, crystals, and a brass locket that, when placed under a microscope, was inscribed with the message - ‘bridging two worlds’.

On one odd occasion, SPR researcher Arthur Ellison reportedly asked to take a materialised crystal with him, only for the unusual souvenir to vanish once he left the cellar. In its place was a small brass plate bearing his full name, which he hadn't then shared with the group.

Extraordinarily, there were also inexplicable newspapers. Freshly printed sheets from the 1940s landed on the table and, perhaps even more wondrously, a paper from three days in the future. When publication day came, it proved to be an exact match.

‌

As a subscriber to The Spiritual Scientist, Dr Willin had the opportunity to attend one of the séances that had sparked such astonishment. He paid £50 for the privilege, which included a light buffet lunch.

Dr Willin, who arrived "excited" to get going, remembered: "They warned us it would be, if I recall, very dark, which it was very dark. And that we were to go in with an open mind, which is more or less what I did."

‌

There were around 10 people in the group, sitting around a table cloaked in darkness like a scene straight out of a Gothic Victorian novel.

"Then there was some music played, which is normal for these sorts of séances. Then slowly but surely, things started to happen," he said. Not long after music began to drift from the cassette player, a silence descended over the group, then came the voices.

"A voice came through one of the mediums. And I think it was a female voice first of all, and then various other voices came through different people, and a jar, I remember, illuminated." There was the opportunity to ask the 'spirit' questions.

‌

In their 450-page report, the SPR researchers testified how voices often filled the darkened room, answering complex scientific questions, as well as ones about private family matters and deceased loved ones, and even engaging in intellectual debates. Some of these voices had names and histories. One of the most frequent 'visitors' was Mrs Emily Bradshaw, a crisply spoken long-dead lady who would even banter heartily with participants.

Fontana wrote: "Emily Bradshaw had jokingly bet Montague Keen half a crown (an old coin no longer used) over some factual matter on which they have disagreed, and when she was proved wrong (much to Montague's triumphant amusement), we heard something clatter onto the floor. After the séance was over, Montague found it was the promised half crown."

‌

The level of detail left researchers stunned, but Dr Willin was left deeply disappointed.

"I asked one of the spirits, 'Is there any music in the spirit world?' And she replied to say, 'Oh yes, you really ought to start studying music. It's fascinating, and music is very relevant in the spirit world, and perhaps you should think about taking up some sort of instrument or something'."

‌

By that time, Melvyn had already earned multiple music degrees and played around six different instruments.

Meanwhile, previous attendees had told of the wonder of a light, which apparently morphed into ghostly faces with moving lips. Some believed these lights could be controlled by thoughts, with SPR members thinking up shapes for the lights to make.

But Dr Willin quickly became 'suspicious' when the light began to flash, shooting this way and that. "When it came within reach of me, I grabbed it, which of course I shouldn't have done, and I trapped it between my two hands.

‌

"It was a very strange sensation, because it was like a long knitting needle, slightly rough, with a light on the end of it. And as I clasped it in my hands, it pulled through my hands and away, and kept away from me for the whole of the rest of the session. It went around other people and went allegedly through them, and they were very impressed with it. But it kept away from me after that."

Many of those who passed through that now-notorious cellar reported highly positive experiences, with some even weeping with joy as they re-entered the world beyond. There were reported lasting transformative effects. Some felt reconnected with their late loved ones, while others claimed their illnesses had been healed.

‌

But for Dr Willin, the experience left him with more questions than answers, and he claims he was promptly banned from future gatherings.

"After the séance, there was a degree of hostility, and I was told that I couldn't go back again," he said. "They said that because I'd broken the rules by grabbing hold of something that was not meant to be grabbed hold of, that I wasn't allowed back. And that I was just trying to cause disruption, which I certainly wasn't doing."

After returning home, Melvyn wrote up his experiences as quickly as possible, while his memory was still fresh, and sent his thoughts off to one of the SPR researchers, as an independent witness. Melvyn recalled: "He replied saying, 'Oh dear, oh dear, you know, you shouldn't have done this, you shouldn't have done that, and I think you've misinterpreted that'.

‌

"Hey, perhaps he was right. I mean, he's unfortunately dead now, but so perhaps I was at fault, who knows. But I did write it all up, and I showed it to people who had had similar experiences, and they said, 'Yes, that's more or less how we interpreted it and what happened'. And the believers said, 'Well, no, perhaps you just went on a bad day, or perhaps you sent out a bad vibe, albeit unconsciously, and that's what caused things to go wrong for your attendance'. So, you know, that's one possibility."

The Scole experiment wrapped up in 1998, with members explaining that interferences with the interdimensional doorway were causing issues. Ellison, Fontana and Keen remained confident in their assessment of The Scole Experiment being unexplainable until they were in graves of their own.

In the years since, nobody has managed to disprove what allegedly occurred in Scole, and even sceptics agree that, if these were just a series of magic tricks, then they were truly phenomenal ones.
